'''John E. Bercaw''' (born December 3, 1944) is an American [[chemist]] and Centennial Professor of Chemistry, Emeritus at the [[California Institute of Technology]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cce.caltech.edu/faculty/bercaw/ |title=FACULTY ::: Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering ::: CALTECH |accessdate=2009-07-15 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20091026002122/http://www.cce.caltech.edu/faculty/bercaw/ |archivedate=2009-10-26 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://directory.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/search.cgi?searchtext=bercaw|title = John e. Bercaw &#124; Caltech Directory}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Born on December 3, 1944 in [[Cincinnati]], Ohio,<ref name="e552">{{cite web | title=Department of Chemistry | website=Illinois | date= | url=https://chemistry.illinois.edu/bailar-lecturer-2002-03-john-e-bercaw | access-date=18 March 2026}}</ref> Bercaw obtained his bachelor of science in 1967 from [[North Carolina State University]] and later his PhD from the [[University of Michigan]] in 1971 under the direction of [[Hans-Herbert Brintzinger]],<ref name="thesis-bercaw-1971">{{cite thesis |title=Titanocene as a reactive intermediate in the reduction of molecular hydrogen and nitrogen |date=1971 |publisher=[[University of Michigan]] |type=Ph.D. |last=Bercaw |first=John Edward |oclc=68280047 |id={{ProQuest|302503406}}}}</ref> followed by [[postdoctoral research]] with [[Jack Halpern (chemist)|Jack Halpern]] at the [[University of Chicago]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.chemistry.illinois.edu/events/lectures/bailar/John_Bercaw.html |title=John e. Bercaw / Chemistry at Illinois |access-date=March 24, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170504224517/http://www.chemistry.illinois.edu/events/lectures/bailar/John_Bercaw.html |archive-date=May 4, 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Career==
He joined the faculty at the Caltech in 1972. Bercaw was elected a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1991.<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780–2010: Chapter B|url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterB.pdf|publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|accessdate=June 15, 2011}}</ref>

He is a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] (elected 1990), and he has received several national awards from the [[American Chemical Society]] (see below).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www2.chemistry.msu.edu/Lectureships/lectures.asp?series=MTR&Year=1993 |title=MSU Chemistry - Max T. Rogers Lectureship |website=www2.chemistry.msu.edu |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040327173720/http://www.chemistry.msu.edu/Lectureships/lectures.asp?series=MTR&Year=1993 |archive-date=2004-03-27}}</ref>

His research interests are in synthetic, structural and mechanistic organotransition metal chemistry, including most recently catalysts for polymerization and trimerization of olefins and investigations of hydrocarbon hydroxylation; fundamental transformations and thermodynamics of organotransition metal chemistry; catalysts for hydrocarbon partial oxidation; catalysts for olefin trimerization and polymerization; homogeneous transformations of carbon monoxide and dihydrogen to fuels and chemicals.

Prof. Bercaw has greatly enhanced understanding of the mechanisms of [[Ziegler–Natta catalyst|Ziegler-Natta]] (ZN) olefin polymerizations. This metal-catalyzed polymerization process is operated on a vast scale and produces, worldwide, over 200 billion pounds of polyolefins per year. Bercaw’s work has led to an understanding of the mechanisms of chain growth in ZN polymerizations and the factors which control [[Syndiotactic#Syndiotactic polymers|syndio-]] and [[Isotactic#Isotactic polymers|isotacticities]] and the degree of comonomer incorporation in copolymerizations; these variables are critical in determining the physical properties of the resultant [[polymers]] and [[copolymers]].

Commercial processes have been based on Bercaw’s discoveries. For example, new and superior ethylene/alpha-olefin copolymers are now industrially produced with titanium catalysts utilizing (η<sup>5</sup>- C<sub>5</sub>Me<sub>4</sub>)SiMe<sub>2</sub>NCMe<sub>3</sub> and related ligands devised in Bercaw’s laboratories. These copolymers have proved to have superior properties. These types of systems have also allowed superior methods for production of [[ethylene]]/[[propylene]] and [[ethylene]]/[[propylene]]/diene [[elastomers]].
